19551.etyen:
Compound of Gess (“G-flat”) + dur (“major”), literally “G-flat major”.
The first element Gess (“G-flat”) is the capitalized form of gess, analyzed by NAOB as g (“G”) + -ess (“flat-note-forming suffix”). The second element dur (“major”) is via German Dur (“major”) from Middle High German bēdūre (“B-natural; hard B”), from Medieval Latin b durum (“hard B”). The adjective is from Latin dūrus (“hard”), from Proto-Italic *dūros (“hard”), from Proto-Indo-European *dweh₂rós (“long, far”), from the root *dweh₂- (“far, long”).
Compare the parallel formations Norwegian Nynorsk Gess-dur, Danish Ges-dur,

en.g: An inflectional suffix forming the definite plural of neuter nouns, corresponding to English “the”

1000287.etyen:
A native Norwegian neuter definite plural ending, incorporated into Bokmål from Norwegian dialects. It belongs to the same inherited system of suffixed definiteness as Etymology 1, although the historical inflectional forms were not identical.
Compare Norwegian Nynorsk -a (“neuter definite plural ending”).

The innermost and largest of Mars's two moons.

1001055.etyen:
Internationalism, borrowed from Ancient Greek Φόβος (Phóbos, “Phobos, personification of fear”), from Ancient Greek φόβος (phóbos, “panic flight; fear”), from Proto-Hellenic Proto-Hellenic *pʰógʷos, from Proto-Indo-European Proto-Indo-European *bʰógʷos, from *bʰegʷ- (“to run, flee”).
The astronomical name commemorates the mythological Fobos, the personification of fear and a companion of Ares; in Hesiod, he is a son of Ares and Aphrodite and the brother of Deimos. The moon was discovered by Asaph Hall in August 1877. The names of Mars's two moons were suggested by the British scholar Henry Geo

en.g: a female given name from Old Norse
x: Torbjørg kommer på besøk i morgen.
Torbjørg is coming to visit tomorrow.
Torbjørg Haugen vet hva Ole Einar Bjørndalen, Marit Bjørgen og Petter Northug spiser for å prestere best.
Torbjørg Haugen knows what Ole Einar Bjørndalen, Marit Bjørgen and Petter Northug eat in order to perform at their best.

1001311.etyen:
Inherited from Old Norse Þorbjǫrg, composed of Þórr (“Thor”) + bjǫrg (“help, protection, salvation”), literally “Thor-protection”.
The first element Þórr is from Proto-Germanic *Þunraz (“Thor, god of thunder”), a personification of *þunraz (“thunder”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *(s)tenh₂- (“to thunder”). The second element bjǫrg is from Proto-Germanic *bergō (“protection, shelter, defense”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *bʰergʰ- (“to protect, preserve”).
Compare Faroese Torbjørg, Icelandic Þorbjörg and Swedish Torbjörg (“female given names”).

en.g: a male given name from Old Norse

1001567.etyen: The given name is of uncertain Nordic origin. It has been treated either as an Old Norse variant of Alfr (“male given name”), from alfr (“elf”), or as a younger form belonging to the name family of Old Norse Alvér, a variant of Ǫlvér. The latter name is also continued in Norwegian as Olve. Its original name elements and meaning are uncertain.

1002079.etyen: From irske (“definite of irsk”) + sjøen (“definite of sjø”).

1004639.etyen:
From the officially standardized Norwegian place-name element Trifan-, representing a local adaptation of Russian Трифон (Trifon), from Ancient Greek Τρύφων (Trúphōn, “delicate; one who lives softly or luxuriously”), ultimately from Ancient Greek τρυφάω (trupháō, “to live softly or luxuriously”), itself from Ancient Greek τρυφή (truphḗ, “softness, delicacy; luxury”), and høgda, the definite feminine singular of høgd or høgde (“hill, rise”). The name refers to Saint Tryphon of Pechenga.
Compare Kven Triffanan- and Northern Sami Triffan-, corresponding place-name elements derived from the same R
